scenes.onScreen: "shared_ptr and weak_ptr": numbered lines (1. Many shared_ptr can own one object; 2. A counter tracks the owners; 3. A weak_ptr looks but does not own) and an analogy card: a Wi-Fi password: many people share it, and the router stays on until the last one leaves
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A shared pointer lets many owners share one object. A counter inside tracks the owners. When the last owner dies, the object is deleted. A weak pointer looks at the object but does not own it. It does not change the counter. Think of a Wi-Fi password. Many people share it, and the router stays on until the last person leaves. Some objects have many owners. A shared pointer fits. It keeps a counter, and it deletes the object when the counter reaches zero. Weak pointer solves a problem. If two objects own each other with shared pointers, neither is ever freed. A weak pointer breaks the circle, because it does not own.
points: Many shared_ptr can own one object
A weak_ptr looks but does not own

scenes.onScreen: shared.cpp: use_count goes up and down
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Make shared builds an int and one shared pointer. [HL 7] The count is one. [HL 9] B is a copy. Copying is allowed here. Both own the int. [HL 10] The count is two. [HL 11] At the closing brace, b dies. [HL 12] The count drops back to one. [HL 6] Make shared builds the object, and the count is one. [HL 7] The use count call reads the count. It prints one. [HL 9] Another shared pointer copies a, so the count grows to two. [HL 12] The inner block ends, b dies, and the count falls back to one.

scenes.onScreen: two shared pointers point at the same int, which keeps a counter
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Here are two owners, a and b. Both point at the same int. A counter next to the int says two. When b dies, the counter becomes one. When a dies, it becomes zero, and the int is deleted. Notice the counter in the middle of the picture. Every new owner adds one, and every owner that leaves takes one away. At zero, the object is freed.

scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] W is a weak pointer. It owns nothing. [HL 8] S owns an int with the value seven. [HL 9] W now watches the same object. [HL 10] Expired asks if the object is gone. Not yet, so zero. [HL 11] Lock gives a shared pointer, if the object is alive. [HL 12] It reads seven. [HL 15] After the block, s is dead. The object is deleted, and expired is one. [HL 6] The weak pointer starts empty. [HL 9] It watches the object, but the count stays the same. [HL 11] Lock gives a shared pointer if the object is alive. If not, it gives an empty pointer. [HL 15] After the block, the object is gone, so expired is true.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as weak dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints zero, seven, and then one. Notice the order. The first expired call gives false. The second one gives true, after the object died.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Many shared pointers can own one object. Two. A counter tracks the owners, and the last owner deletes the object. Three. A weak pointer watches without owning. Four. Lock turns a weak pointer into a shared pointer, or an empty one. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Many shared pointers can own one object.
A counter tracks the owners, and the last owner deletes the object.
A weak pointer watches without owning.
Lock turns a weak pointer into a shared pointer, or an empty one.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A raw pointer into a shared_ptr
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We assign a raw new result to a shared pointer. The compiler says it cannot convert int star to shared pointer. Use make shared instead. It builds the object and the counter in one safe step. The constructor of a shared pointer is explicit, so the equals sign does not work. Do not wrap a raw pointer by hand. Use make shared. It is shorter, it is safe, and it does one memory request instead of two.

scenes.onScreen: Shared pointers are polite. The last one out always turns off the light.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

shared.cpp: In function 'int main()':
shared.cpp:6:25: error: conversion from 'int*' to non-scalar type 'std::shared_ptr<int>' requested
    6 |     shared_ptr<int> a = new int(5);
      |                         ^~~~~~~~~~
bug.why: The shared pointer constructor from a raw pointer is explicit, so an equals sign does not work. Make shared is also faster and safer.

pun: "Shared pointers are polite. The last one out always turns off the light."
challenge: Make a shared pointer to an int. Copy it into a second shared pointer. Print use count. Hint: the count is one after the first pointer, and two after the copy.
challengeAnswer: Use make shared for the first. Write the second as a copy of the first. Use count prints two.
